records.name: Rio de Jeneiro
records.summary:
Rio de Janeiro recorded only 3 trans killings in 2025 (a low rate of ~0.18/million against a population of ~17 M), well below the national average. However, two distinct visitor-facing signals pull the score modestly below the national 0.71: a documented extortion pattern in Niterói and a tourist-targeting scam in Copacabana.

In January–February 2026, multiple trans sex workers in central Niterói reported a two-year coercive regime: a man claiming militia and public-agent connections forced them to pay R$120 per week each and had 'almost strangled three of the girls.' The alleged extorter was an ex-employee of Niterói city hall, arrested in 'Operação Ronda Sumbria' by the 76ª DP, and remanded in pre-trial custody. The institutional response was mixed—arrests and dismissal occurred, but the racket operated under the appearance of state backing for roughly two years before intervention. Trans council member Benny Briolly brought the case to the Public Ministry.

Separately, in Copacabana the tourist police (Deat) arrested two trans women caught extorting a Norwegian tourist with threats to circulate intimate videos—a documented, visitor-facing scam vector. The killing rate is low, but the coercive pattern with state implication and the tourist-targeting scam justify a deviation of about 0.03 below national. Compared with São Paulo (no deviation), Rio's risk is qualitative rather than numerical.

records.name: Goias
records.summary:
Goiás recorded 5 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, placing it in the national mid-band alongside Maranhão and Pará. Against a population of ~7.2 million the rate is about 0.69 per million per year, roughly 1.8× the national rate (80 killings across ~211 million). Goiás sits on the Cerrado agricultural frontier, and the ANTRA dossier finds 67.5% of Brazilian trans killings occur in interior cities outside the capitals - where monitoring, reporting and access to public policy are weaker - so a visitor away from the capital shares this interior exposure.

No Goiás-specific ordinance, legal restriction or protection measure was identified in the dossier; the state's risk profile rests on the above-national per-capita killing count and the interior-concentration pattern. The companion 2024 national dossier (122 killings, 16% below 2023) recorded the same ~68% outside-capitals share.

records.name: Maranhao
records.summary:
Maranhão recorded 5 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025 — the same count the association dossier logged for it in 2024 — so its position in the ranking's middle-upper band is persistent rather than a one-year spike (SBT News, 26 January 2026; CNN Brasil, 27 January 2025). No Maranhão-specific statute, ordinance or enforcement policy affecting trans people is documented in the audited sources; federal law applies uniformly.

The national profile the dossiers attach to this state's region — victims young, Black, poor and Northeastern; 97% travestis and trans women; most killings in public places, at night, and outside state capitals where monitoring and policy access are thinner — maps onto Maranhão's place in both tables. The documented risk is structural exposure: two consecutive years of above-median lethal counts in a country that leads the world's tallies, without any local legal change either way.

records.name: Para
records.summary:
Pará recorded 5 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, in the middle band of the ANTRA dossier's state ranking of that year's 80 national killings (SBT News, 26 January 2026). No Pará-specific statute, ordinance or policy affecting trans people was found in the audited sources; the federal framework applies uniformly. The second audited source lists the 2024 worst-hit states without naming this state, so its 2024 position cannot be fixed from the record.

What the dossiers do document bears directly on a vast Amazonian state: roughly two-thirds to 68% of such killings nationally occur in interior cities outside the capitals, where monitoring, denunciation and access to public policy are weaker, and victims are overwhelmingly young Black travestis and trans women killed in public places. For a trans visitor travelling beyond the main metropolitan area, the least-monitored geography is precisely where the recorded killings sit.

records.name: Alagoas
records.summary:
Alagoas recorded 6 killings of trans and travesti people in 2024 — among the elevated small-state totals in that year's ANTRA dossier table (CNN Brasil, 27 January 2025) — and 2 in 2025 (SBT News, 26 January 2026). No Alagoas-specific legal restriction or enforcement finding is documented; federal law applies uniformly.

The swing between consecutive dossiers on a small population is itself the finding: at these denominators a couple of cases moves a state's position sharply, which is why the monitoring body cautions that falling national counts reflect violence shifting into attempted homicides and persistent under-recording (misclassification of victims' gender identity degrades the data) rather than improving safety. The victim profile the dossiers attach to this region — young, Black, poor, Northeastern, killed in public places at night — places risk wherever a visibly trans person is in public, in a state inside the country's hardest-hit region.

records.name: Mato Grosso
records.summary:
Mato Grosso recorded 3 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025 on a population of ~3.6 million - about 0.83 per million per year, more than double the national rate, and the 2024 dossier counted 8 killings in the state, its highest year. The state sits on the Cerrado/agribusiness frontier, where the dossier's finding that most killings happen outside the capitals means small-town exposure is relevant for visitors travelling beyond Cuiabá.

Three cases on a small population is statistically fragile, and no qualitative incident, ordinance or enforcement evidence was found beyond the ANTRA counts; the elevated per-capita reading therefore carries a smaller weight than the raw rate suggests.

records.name: Distrito Federal
records.summary:
The Distrito Federal recorded 2 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, a low absolute count for a major metropolitan area. Brasília is the seat of the STF, the national protective apparatus, and the offices of human-rights bodies; ANTRA's own Dossiê is compiled and reported from DF desks. The capital hosts international diplomatic missions and NGO infrastructure that raise the visibility and institutional cost of anti-trans violence.

These factors justify a modest positive deviation of about 0.02 above the national 0.71. Compared with São Paulo (0.71, no deviation), which also leads in institutional capacity but recorded 4 killings in 2025 and 16 in 2024, the DF's lower absolute numbers and concentration of protective infrastructure make it marginally safer for a visitor. The 2 killings against ~3 million population give a rate of ~0.67/million—above the national average in per-capita terms—so the positive deviation is qualitative (institutional visibility, international presence) rather than purely numerical.

records.name: Sachsen
records.summary:
Two documented 2025 features raise Sachsen above the German norm for visitor risk around queer visibility: neo-Nazis mounted a counter-protest intended to disrupt Dresden's pride march on 31 May 2025 (the march proceeded); and the state government, with two neighbouring states, co-sponsored a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act after an abuse-of-self-ID court case ('Fall Liebich'), alleging misuse of the self-ID right — an organised, multi-state push to roll back trans self-determination law.

Germany's national protections and functioning rule of law apply unchanged here; the documented counter-action was policed without event cancellation or reported injuries. Earlier assertions of a wider multi-city attack pattern (Bautzen mob sizes, Döbeln prosecutions) lack support in the retained sources and are removed from the record.
